fit.tex:
Measuring $\mathcal{I}(p)$ for $p=1,\dots,20$ on the model networks (Fig.~\ref{fig:model_dim}) shows that the first effect dominates almost everywhere: $\mathcal{I}$ falls monotonically with $p$ for every model except the two regular lattices, and it does not saturate. At $p=20$ the
Erd\text{\H{o}}s--R\text{\'{e}}nyi graph reaches $\mathcal{I}=3\times10^{-7}$, the range occupied by the lattices at $p=2$. There is accordingly no characteristic dimension beyond which the measure
levels off, and we do not interpret $\mathcal{I}(p)$ as an estimator of an intrinsic embedding dimension. Two observations make that reading untenable. First, the shortest-path metric is not Euclidean-realizable at any small $p$: the hop distance on a square grid is the $\ell_1$ metric, which admits no isometric Euclidean embedding in any dimension, and the residual stress correspondingly plateaus at a nonzero value ($2607$ for the $10\times10$ grid) rather than vanishing. Second, the one model whose generative dimension is known---a random geometric graph drawn in the plane---shows no feature at $p=2$ whatsoever; its stress falls by more than half between $p=2$ and $p=3$ and $\mathcal{I}$ decreases monotonically throughout.

shape.tex:
Because the pairwise-distance matrix $D^{(m)}$ of a run is invariant under
$\mathrm{E}(p)$, terminal configurations can be compared without alignment. We
use the scale-free distance
%
\begin{equation}
  \Delta_{mn}
  \;=\;\frac{\big\lVert D^{(m)}-D^{(n)}\big\rVert_{F}}
            {\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\lVert D^{(m)}\rVert_{F}+\lVert D^{(n)}\rVert_{F}\big)} ,
  \label{eq:run_distance}
\end{equation}
%
which is defined without reference to the curvature of
Sec.~\ref{sec:curvature}. Keeping the two independent matters: a merge threshold
derived from $\lambda_{\min}$ would make the grouping a function of the very
quantity it is meant to be compared against, and the stopping tolerance of the
optimizer does not supply such a threshold either, being a tolerance on the
relative improvement of the stress rather than a bound on the distance to a
minimizer.

hessian.tex:
Two properties govern how $H$ may be read. First, the $p$ translations are exact
null directions at any configuration, because the stress depends only on
coordinate differences. The $p(p-1)/2$ rotations are null directions of $H$ only
at a stationary point: the stress is constant along the rotation orbit, so
$v^{\mathsf{T}}Hv=-\nabla F_G\!\cdot\!X''(0)$, which vanishes only when
$\nabla F_G=0$. We therefore project the rigid-motion tangent space out of $H$
rather than assuming $p(p+1)/2$ null eigenvalues, and we report the norm of the
projected gradient at every terminal configuration as a stationarity diagnostic
alongside the number of iterations used and whether the iteration budget was
binding. We write $\lambda_{\min}$ for the smallest eigenvalue of the projected
Hessian and, because $\lambda_{\min}$ carries the scale of $H$ and hence depends
on $N$, we report the dimensionless ratio
%
\begin{equation}
  \widetilde{\lambda}_{\min}
  \;=\;\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\operatorname{tr}(H_{+})/(Np-q)},
  \qquad q=\tfrac{1}{2}p(p+1),
  \label{eq:lam_rel}
\end{equation}
%
where $H_{+}$ denotes the positive part of the projected spectrum.

rigidity.tex:
Second, in the zero-residual limit $\delta_{ij}=d_{ij}$ the second term of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:hess_block} vanishes and $H=2R^{\mathsf{T}}WR$ with $R$ a rigidity
matrix. The framework in question is the \emph{complete} one: the stress imposes
a dissimilarity on every node pair, not on the edges of $G$. Sparsity of $G$
therefore does not make the framework underconstrained, since a complete
framework is generically rigid for $N>p+1$.

The intra-state scale is therefore measured rather than derived. Each terminal
configuration is re-optimized under a tighter setting and then perturbed and
re-optimized several times; the distribution of $\Delta$ among returns to the
same configuration sets the scale below which two runs are not distinguishable.
We do not report a grouping at a single threshold. Instead we scan the threshold
over a range and report the interval on which the number of groups is stable,
and we retain only groups that recur when the procedure is repeated on an
independent batch of seeds, with the medoids of the first batch used to assign
the second.

morse.tex:
Accordingly we report a small
$\lambda_{\min}$ as a near-zero projected curvature mode and make no claim of a
continuous floppy manifold; establishing one requires continuation along the
corresponding eigenvector to exhibit an actual low-stress path.

$\beta$ is informative only away from its two degenerate limits. If every run
forms its own group the within term is zero by construction and $\beta=1$
identically; if all runs form one group $\beta=0$ identically. Both hold for any
data whatsoever, so a value at either extreme reports the grouping and not the
landscape. We therefore quote $\beta$ only together with the group-size
distribution and the stability interval of Sec.~\ref{sec:clustering}, and we
treat a partition into singletons as the statement that no two sampled terminal
configurations were merged at the thresholds examined, which is weaker than a
count of distinct minima.

multiplicity.tex:
We treat embedding variability as a diagnostic observable of a specified graph-to-embedding procedure. Random initialization is the sampling device; even when it is the only stochastic input (initial position), the dispersion of terminal outputs can depend on the graph via the deterministic stress-minimization map. Accordingly, we test for differences between observed graphs and matched null ensembles under a common protocol, rather than posing algorithmic and structural variation as mutually exclusive alternatives.

We use the term embedding multistability operationally to denote initialization-sensitive terminal geometries under this protocol. A multibasin interpretation requires additional evidence from terminal-state lustering, final stresses, and local curvature; NEI alone is not a count of
minima and does not prove uniqueness when it is small.

The intra-state scale is therefore measured rather than derived. Each terminal
configuration is re-optimized under a tighter setting and then perturbed and
re-optimized several times; the distribution of $\Delta$ among returns to the
same configuration sets the scale below which two runs are not distinguishable.
We do not report a grouping at a single threshold. Instead we scan the threshold
over a range and report the interval on which the number of groups is stable,
and we retain only groups that recur when the procedure is repeated on an
independent batch of seeds, with the medoids of the first batch used to assign
the second.

rigid.tex: For the regular-lattice benchmarks examined here, all sampled initializations converged to terminal configurations whose pairwise-distance matrices were indistinguishable within numerical tolerance, yielding \(\mathcal{I}\) values near the numerical floor. Second, from our real network analysis, most results show that the three-tier ordering $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{real}} < \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{deg}} < \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ER}}$ holds across network categories: if NEI were dominated by optimizer noise, this systematic dependence on higher-order structural correlations would not be expected. The near-zero NEI obtained from Kamada--Kawai layouts (Appendix~\ref{appendix:layout_comparison}) should be read as a protocol dependence, not as a failure of the measure: under our implementation and convergence settings, repeated KK runs yield essentially identical configurations, so the associated stress landscape reveals no accessible multi-basin structure. NEI is by construction a property of a specified stress function and sampling protocol; we therefore restrict the physical interpretation to SMACOF-MDS, for which the objective and initialization ensemble are explicitly defined.

\caption{Protocol dependence of the average NEI for the model networks. The first four columns vary two \texttt{scikit-learn} settings independently. \texttt{n\_init} is the number of independent SMACOF starts kept per ensemble member: the library default of four returns only the lowest-stress draw, which samples a different measure from the single-start basin occupancy of Eq.~\eqref{eq:basin_occupancy}. $\varepsilon$ is the stress tolerance. The last column applies a fixed-budget first-order optimizer instead. The two settings fail in different regimes: on rugged landscapes (ER, BA, HK, SBM) neither changes $\mathcal{I}$ by more than about 20\%, whereas keeping the best of four starts narrows the ensemble by a factor of 40 for the random geometric graph, and a loose tolerance inflates the two regular lattices by three orders of magnitude. The lattices are therefore the diagnostic: their unique minimizer forces $\mathcal{I}\to0$ only at convergence, so a large value in those rows signals an unconverged optimization rather than a property of the topology.}

unresolved.tex:
The average NEI is a mean, over node pairs, of a run-to-run variance, and a
variance can be large for structurally distinct reasons. Two topologies with the
same $\mathcal{I}$ may differ in whether the ensemble settled in several
separated configurations, or in a single configuration that is free to deform at
almost no cost in stress. The scalar does not distinguish these. This section
introduces two diagnostics that address them separately. Neither replaces
$\mathcal{I}$; they identify what produced a given value.

$\beta$ is informative only away from its two degenerate limits. If every run
forms its own group the within term is zero by construction and $\beta=1$
identically; if all runs form one group $\beta=0$ identically. Both hold for any
data whatsoever, so a value at either extreme reports the grouping and not the
landscape. We therefore quote $\beta$ only together with the group-size
distribution and the stability interval of Sec.~\ref{sec:clustering}, and we
treat a partition into singletons as the statement that no two sampled terminal
configurations were merged at the thresholds examined, which is weaker than a
count of distinct minima.
